subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
subsubtopic: COVERAGE OF QUEBEC ELECTION-FAILURE OF FRENCH NETWORK TO INVITE PRIME MINISTER TO COMMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following many questions asked about the reporting on election night in Quebec, I received this morning from the CBC a report on each of the three points raised. With the consent of the House, I would like to make its content known to hon. members, since it seems to me that the text is a little too long for the oral question period itself and that you could hardly authorize me to read it.
As for the broadcasting time granted to party leaders on election night, the CBC has given me the following information: We devoted 20 minutes and 54 seconds of television broadcasting time to cover the news from Liberal headquarters on election night. Of that time, 8 minutes and 34 seconds were used to describe the atmosphere at the committee rooms, the arrival of the victorious leader and the ovation he received from his supporters: on that occasion, the new premier made a statement that lasted 6 minutes and 35 seconds which was carried in full. He later agreed to an interview that lasted 5 minutes and 20 seconds.
The leader of the Union nationale had decided to wait for the results at his home in the riding of Missisquoi. We obtained a statement from him; it lasted 2 minutes and 51 seconds and he agreed to answer questions for 2 minutes and 10 seconds.
The leader of the Ralliement Creditiste refused to make a statement. He preferred granting us an interview of 7 minutes and 5 seconds. We proposed to Mr. Samson to cover the statement he would make before
his supporters on election night. He turned down our invitation because he preferred a studio interview.
The Parti quebecois had invited its supporters and the public to follow the events on election night at the Paul Sauve arena. That is where Mr. Levesque had decided to make a statement before his supporters and to give us an interview. He delivered a speech of 11 minutes and 40 seconds-which we did broadcast in full-and gave us an interview that lasted 4 minutes and 35 seconds.
Needless to say, the CBC did not have any control over the length of speeches made by each leader to his supporters or on his statement to the electorate. Had Mr. Bertrand made a 10-minute statement, we would have carried it in full and we would have done the same for Mr. Bourassa had he made a 15-minute speech before his supporters.
We had also invited to our broadcasting studios candidates from each party: four from the Union nationale, four Liberals' three from the Parti quebecois, three Creditistes and one NDP. Only two Union nationale representatives came to our studio. It was the same for the Quebec Liberal party and Parti quebecois. No Creditiste representative showed up as arranged, on election night. The New Democratic party representative came.
The Prime Minister of Canada was not invited to our public affairs broadcasts following the Quebec provincial elections and this for a simple reason. We took for granted, as the Prime Minister's office had indicated on voting day, that it was against tradition for a federal prime minister to comment the results of a provincial election. Under the circumstances, no special invitation was extended to the Prime Minister of Canada to take part in a public affairs broadcast on the results of the Quebec elections.
9 (2:10 p.m.)
Besides, going as far back into the past as we can, we do not remember the French network ever inviting the Prime Minister of the country on a public affairs program following a provincial election in Quebec.
However, the words spoken by Mr. Trudeau upon his arrival in Parliament, the day after
May 11. 1970

Yukon and Territorial Lands Acts the election, were included in our news broadcasts, either as background stories or interviews with him. We did not think it advisable to add to this interview, which was part of our radio and television news broadcasts, a special public affairs program at which he would have been a guest.
All the more so as, with regard to the anniversary of Mr. Trudeau's and the Liberal government's accession to power, we had contacted the Prime Minister's office as early as April 13, to invite him to give an appreciation of his two years of administration on radio. A television program on the same subject was to have taken place later.
Finally, the CBC did not cover the meeting of Creditiste members of the provincial Parliament which is supposed to have taken place in Quebec on May 2 simply because, like all other media, it was completely unaware of that meeting. The news editors of the following newspapers and television stations were not informed of the Creditiste caucus held in Quebec: Le Soleil, L'Action, Le Journal de Quebec, La Presse, Channel 4, CHRC, CJRT, CKCV. Moreover, the leader of the Ralliement creditiste himself, Mr. Camil Samson, admitted that this was an in camera meeting not to be followed by a statement to the press.
All the news editors of the different media complain of the great difficulty in properly covering the activities of the Ralliement creditiste because of the Ralliement's almost complete lack of a press service.
It might be added that, in the circumstances, the CBC is in the same boat as private radio and television stations and newspapers, none of which referred that weekend to the Creditiste meeting.

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-MONITORING OF CONVERSATIONS BETWEEN INMATE AND VISITOR
PENITENTIARIES-MONITORING OF CONVERSATIONS BETWEEN INMATE AND VISITOR
speechtext:
1.	Is it the policy of the government, that conversations between inmates of federal prisons and their visitors be monitored by prison authorities and, if so, at which federal prisons in British Columbia is this done?
2.	Is it the policy of the government, that prisoners, when speaking with visitors, be restricted as to what language they may speak and, if so (a) what are these restrictions (b) by prison, what restrictions are applied in the federal prisons of British Columbia?
3.	Have Indian prisoners at federal prisons in British Columbia been instructed to stop conversing with visitors in their native tongue and to continue only in French or in English and, if so, at which prisons?
May 11, 1970

4.	By prison, how many officials of the federal prisons of British Columbia, are familiar with the French language?

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-MONITORING OF CONVERSATIONS BETWEEN INMATE AND VISITOR
speechtext:
1.
The policy, as set out in sections 2.17 and 2.18 of Penitentiary Service Regulations, provides that the visiting privileges that may be permitted to inmates shall be such as are, in all circumstances calculated to assist in the reformation and rehabilitation of the inmate; also, that insofar as practicable the privacy of visits shall be maintained but that nothing therein shall be deemed to limit supervision of visiting to the extent considered necessary or desirable for the reformation and rehabilitation of inmates or the security of the institution. In the supervision of visiting monitoring of conversations occurs but in those institutions only and to the extent only considered necessary for such supervision. The British Columbia Penitentiary (New Westminster) is the only Federal prison in British Columbia in which there is provision for monitoring conversations between inmates and visitors.
2.	No, except in special circumstances where arrangements are made for interpreters should one or other of the official languages not be known to either inmate or visitor.

speechtext: Has the federal government promised financial assistance to any Canadian city proposing to host the 1976 Olympic Summer or Winter Games, and, if so, what amount of financial assistance is proposed and for what purposes would such be earmarked?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):

subtopic: SPORTS-FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR 1976 OLYMPIC GAMES
speechtext:
Yes; the Federal Government promised financial assistance to Vancouver, through the Garibaldi Olympic Development Association. Should the bid be successful, Cabinet has agreed to grant $10,000,000 in the form of a fixed grant toward the deficit of a corporation to be established to operate and manage the Winter Olympic Games, providing the Province of British Columbia and the City of Vancouver agree to offset the remaining portion of an anticipated deficit. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 55-STEPS TO INCREASE CONSUMER PURCHASING POWER AND COMBAT INFLATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should take all necessary steps to increase
May 11. 1970	COMMONS
consumer purchasing power to meet their need and to improve the flow of goods in Canada through the use of techniques designed to check rising costs and combat inflation.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it was after serious consideration that the Ralliement creditiste decided to introduce the motion now before the House.
Mr. Speaker, when going through the commercial section of Canadian cities, we are amazed to see that the counters and windows of all department stores and even of small shops are chock-full of products, of merchandise of all kinds, in one word, of commodities that the consumers want and that are good for them, in the sectors of food, clothing, furniture, housing, sports and leisure, culture and entertainment.
Yet, there are no buyers for those commodities everyone wants. In desperation, business owners strain their ingenuity to find ways of attracting customers. They are even prepared to take a small deposit on credit sales.
While there is an excess of stocks over demand and purchasing power, some plants are operating at 60, 70 or 80 per cent of their capacity, particularly in the textile, shoe and automobile industries.
Other plants announce temporary lay-offs for one or two weeks or even longer. In Montreal, an article in La Presse of May 6, announces the closing of the Canadian General Electric plant for two weeks from May 25. A thousand workers will be laid-off on that date.
On the other hand, a bulletin dated May 8 from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics shows that the sale of cars has continued to decrease during March and indicates a decline of 17.3 per cent compared to the corresponding month last year.
In spite of those facts, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the governor of the Bank of Canada still maintain and this for the benefit of the fight against inflation, that total consumer demand is in excess. This merely means that we are buying too much, according to the minister.
Now when stores and warehouses are full, plants are closing and reducing their production to a minimum, it is surely not because there is an excess demand, but it is due to the fact that consumers do not have the necessary purchasing power. Very obvious facts contradict the Finance Minister's statements, Mr. Speaker. There is an abundance of products
DEBATES	6797
Consumer Purchasing Power and Inflation to meet all requirements. However, this aim cannot be reached on account of the lack of money of potential buyers who are therefore unable to purchase at present prices the goods which would satisfy their needs. You may say, "They still do it". At times they succeed for a while in satisfying their needs at the expense of running into debt through credit buying. This is a general situation as anyone can see that a great portion of the population is snowed under with bills.
A bulletin published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics states that, according to answers received, indebtedness reached a partial total of $10,062 million at the end of January 1970, compared to $9,049 million at the end of January 1969, that is a rise of 11.2 per cent in 12 months.
Mr. Speaker, finance and loan companies are the ones who have benefitted from this increase of more than $1 billion in Canadian indebtedness between January 1969 and January 1970.
In the field of personal loans, for instance, the increase in 1969 exceeded $200 million, or 33J per cent. Besides, as the banks are restricting credit and the finance companies have more difficulties in obtaining capital for loans, Canadians are mortgaging their insurance policies.
In the 1969-70 fiscal year life insurance companies have seen their loans on policies increase from $556 to $645 million, namely a rise of 17.1 per cent. That is one of the effects of the government policy on prices and of its fight against inflation: sustained indebtedness. The fact that the population in general is running into debt is another sign that purchasing power is lacking. People are trying by every possible means to improve the situation, even agreeing to pay very high rates of interest.
Mr. Speaker, this is alarming and it greatly worries responsible organizations like the Canadian Welfare Council which has just published a study on the matter. I would like to quote the following extract:
These findings come from an investigation carried out in Hamilton on 235 low income families.
The report points out that a quarter of these families have debts amounting to over 25 per cent of their gross annual income.
When they have paid for food, clothing, rent and debts, these families have only $40.00 left a month.
More than one family out of five in the families sampled live below the poverty line, as determined by the Economic Council of Canada. Their expenses are noticeably higher than authorized by the income at their disposal to resort to credit.

Moreover, the report suggests that the possibility to grant low interest rate loans, guaranteed by the government, to low income families should be considered.
Here is, Mr. Speaker, another consequence of the desastrous government policy as regards the rise in prices and the fight against inflation. Canadian families get more and more into debts, in order to satisfy their needs, and this at such a rate that the Canadian Welfare Council thought advisable to advocate granting with the guarantee of the government, low interest rate loans to low income families in order to get them out of the predicament in which a lot of them find themselves owing to credit restriction policies and the rise in interest rates.
We could talk about people on fixed income, such as pensioners, family and welfare allowance recipients, small non-unionized labourers-and God knows how many there are-who do not have the necessary powers of persuasion to get the salary increases that would allow them to purchase a variety of goods and services that the fruit of then-labour brought them not long ago.
As far as the beneficiaries of family allowances and old age pensions are concerned, the government continues to turn a deaf ear to their demands.
We are short of goods and services? Can we not ensure additional goods and services to these underprivileged classes?
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
No, because affluence does exist. The only thing lacking is the ownership. But the situation is still worse. Even though families are forced into debt in order to cope with rising prices and meet their most legitimate needs, that is not enough to save dealers, contractors and manufacturers from bankruptcy.
On April 8 last, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics published a summary study of business failures in Canada for these last few months, from which I quote:
According to tentative figures, there were 769 bankruptcies during the fourth quarter of 1969. This figure represents an increase of 19 per cent over the figure for the corresponding period in 1968, when the number of bankruptcies was 645. Liabilities of bankrupt firms were estimated at $62,697,000, i.e. 49 per cent more than the $41,901,000 for the corresponding quarter in 1968.
There we have, Mr. Speaker, the rather gloomy picture of the Canadian economy as a result of the government's policies regarding credit and the fight against inflation.

For instance, an analysis of the labour statistics issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics reveals that the number of persons employed increased by 20,000 from February to March, 1970 and that the number of unemployed increased by 16,000 to reach the figure of 542,000 while in the previous years, for the same period, the number of unemployed had shown little change and sometimes had even decreased.
If this analysis is carried out further, it shows that, compared to last year, the labour force has increased by 148,000 workers, or by 1.9 per cent. Over the same period, the number of persons employed has increased by only 54,000, or %o of one per cent while the number of unemployed increased by 94,000 over the previous year.
It is therefore obvious that the government's policy to fight inflation is disastrous for the Canadian workers and the Canadian families, because it contributes to increased unemployment and greater hardship for a larger number of Canadian families.
This is why in my view we have to criticize the government's policy with respect to prices and to inflation. Indeed this policy is weakening more and more the Canadian economy. For this reason among others the Ralliement creditiste condemns the policy of the government and urges the cabinet to take efficient measures to control the rise in prices and inflation so that Canadians can enjoy a better life and more security.
Anyway the Creditistes are not alone in asserting that this policy of restrictions, of increased unemployment, of indebtedness and bankruptcy, which is wanted by the government, in order to fight inflation, has disastrous effects, because it is wrong, pernicious and unrealistic.
One of the thinkers of the federal Liberal party, who now sits in the other place, hon. Senator Maurice Lamontagne, recently gave a piece of his mind to the people who control and promote government policies in a speech he delivered to the shareholders of the Canadian Corporate Management Company, which was published almost verbatim in Le Devoir of April 23 last. Here is what the hon. senator said in part when dealing with the policies of the Canadian Minister of Finance and of the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
Quoting the Minister of Finance, senator Lamontagne said, and I quote:
If we had only to concern ourselves with the over-all demend on our productive capacity and on our markets, no further action would be necessary.
May 11, 1970	COMMONS
But the government announced right after his intention to tighten consumer credit, which can only result in dealing a new blow to the poorest citizens and weakening even further the sector of the economy which is already the weakest, that is the industry of durable consumer goods.
The governor of the Bank of Canada spoke in the same vein when he wrote in his report, and I quote:
The purpose of restraint is not to slow down the economy for its own sake but as a means of slowing down the price and cost increase in order to provide a solid base for sustainable economic expansion.
Senator Lamontagne went on to say that the present Liberal government policies are aberrant, illogical and erroneous. I quote:
Those statements (Mr. Benson's and Mr. Rasmin-sky's) and similar ones made in the United States, in particular by Mr. Arthur Burns, make me wonder about the concept that was generally accepted after the war with regards to fiscal and monetary policies in the fight against inflation.
I feel that we are witnessing in that field, and this in several countries of the western world, including perhaps the United States, the worst aberration since the depression of the '30s.
Senator Lamontagne, at one time economic adviser to the former prime minister, at one time minister in the Liberal government, and who now sits in the other place as an influential member of the Liberal party, claims that the policy of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and that of the governor of the Bank of Canada are aberrant, illogical, erroneous. He added, and I quote:
-that those policies are leading us to the economic stagnation of the 1930s.
And he closed saying:
I have no hesitation in saying that the fiscal and monetary policies of the cyclical type designed to reduce demand, constitute an awkward, inefficient and unrealistic way of combatting an evil stemming mainly from structural and permanent causes in supply.
According to Senator Lamontagne, inflation, price increases derive from structural and permanent causes. Now, it would be interesting to know what are those permanent and structural causes. We are therefore dealing with the present structures, which are the cause of the increase in prices and which are permanent.
In a lecture entitled "INFLATION, its causes and its consequences", Dr. Rosario Cousineau, director of the Department of Commerce of the University of Sherbrooke, stressed the main causes of inflation at the
DEBATES	6799
Consumer Purchasing Power and Inflation conference of the Chamber of Commerce of the province of Quebec. I shall quote three of the main causes mentioned by professor Cousineau:
1.	Combines, Trusts and Monopolies:
Modern technique calls for heavy investments and leads to the creation of big enterprises. Small enterprise can only subsist in such fields where manufacturing calls for the personal care of the craftsman or in cases where it remains the provider of parts and accessories for big industry.
The danger here is that big enterprises could absorb their suppliers and competitors. Economists and sociologists charge that combines, trusts and monopolies are the cause of inflation. They are often right to the extent that the enterprises monopolize natural resources and avail themselves of their privileged conditions to increase their prices and extend their profit margin, without any supplementary allotment of salaries-
2.	Taxes and duties of all kinds:
Public expenditures are another cause of inflation. The liberalities of public powers give way to taxes and duties that weigh heavily on the price of products and personal incomes. As a result, consumer prices increase without any corresponding increase in purchasing power.
3.	Bank and monetary policy:
I do not intend to debate whether banks create money, but we can assert that they do create credit, that they multiply their deposits and their own assets 10 or 15 times (16 at the present time).
That is another cause of inflation.
As reported on page 2740 of the minutes of proceedings of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, the governor of the Bank of Canada referred to those who believe that the rise in interest rates increases costs, without making too much of that fact. I quote part of his statement:
I know the view is sometimes expressed that high interest rates are themselves inflationary because they increase costs of those who do succeed in borrowing money.
And he added that the rise in interests is meant to prompt people to spend less or not at all.
This is Mr. Rasminsky's opinion which senator Lamontagne considers preposterous, unrealistic, not to say stupid. However, Mr. Rasminsky may well say that the interest rates are being increased so as to prompt people to abstain from borrowing and spending, the fact remains that the industrialist who is sure of making a 20 or 25 per cent profit on a given production is not bothered too much by the interest payable on his loans, even at 10 per cent.

The result is a loss in purchasing power which is constantly increasing, as a result of higher interest cost, because of depreciation allowances and fixed costs.
To remedy the situation, we must increase the purchasing power of consumers with new credits which are not included in the costs or in the prices. Those new credits could take the form of payments made directly to all Canadian consumers or by lowering prices, they could increase the purchasing power.
In the first case, it is a national dividend, in the second, the compensated discount which the Creditistes are calling for.
Why these two proposals? As explained earlier, the national dividend does not constitute new money because it is not included in prices and it will not lead to price increases. Certain dealers however, realizing that consumers would have more money, might be tempted to take advantage of the situation by boosting their prices.
Any serious monetary reform must therefore take this human factor into account and

establish the machinery capable of checking unjustified price increases. To this end, Social Crediters advocate a technique likely to check inflation.
Besides, here is what major Douglas had to say before the Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce in Ottawa in 1934, and I quote:
It is possible to apply an increased purchasing power to a price decrease. One of those means is through subsidies. For instance, subsidies are paid to butter producers so that the price of that commodity will not increase.

However, the subsidy can be provided by creating a new purchasing power, that is by doing like banks when they make loans while creating credit. Nobody has ever claimed that if the merchant marine is subsidized, an increase in shipping rates will ensue. To the contrary, they will decrease. What the minister refuses to admit, is that there are two kinds of inflation: the one to which he refers, where demand is greater than supply, and the one to which he never refers, which results from structural and permanent causes in the field of supply.
I would like to point out to the minister that the inflation to which he refers is not a conjunctural but a structural inflation. It is therefore imperative to change the structures.
The present problem is a problem of demand and the minister knows it.
Keynes, the economist, whose philosophy has been acknowledged by most of the free world countries and has inspired the thought of the Canadian government and of the Minister of Finance, has convinced the world that the problem arose not from production but from demand. We know what the present picture is in Canada. The level of unemployment across the nation stands at 6.7 per cent. The government's stated objective in terms of its economic policies is to carry on an anti-inflationary program. According to the latest figures, the consumer price index stood at 128.9 in March of 1970 as compared with 123.2 in March of 1969. This is an increase of 5.7 points, or 4.6 per cent. I am all for trying if there is any chance of success, but when the facts prove that you are playing an impossible game, where many of the causes of inflation are beyond your control, then the argument that we should keep on trying is really an excuse for not providing justice to old age pensioners and others who are being hurt by inflation. As long as we continue to keep on trying beyond a reasonable level, and as long as we hold up the carrot that we can cure inflation, obviously logic dictates that we do not have to do anything about redressing the program we now have. It becomes an excuse for not doing so.
Many years ago in Montreal I listened to Professor Jack Weldon, an economist who was very much alone at that time. He is no longer alone because many economists have accepted the position he advocated. At that time, he pointed out the great danger that attends a policy which concentrates totally on inflation without looking at the other problems created in the process of fighting inflation. He pointed out that the western world would have to learn to live with this particular phenomena and make adjustments accordingly.
Other countries have made adjustments. Japan had a rate of inflation almost three or four times as great as that of Canada, yet the economy of that country has grown at an enormous rate. The Japanese have made the necessary adjustments and have lived with them. They have not priced themselves out of the world markets, certainly not out of Canada's markets. Too many Canadian people are affected by Japanese imports to use that argument. It is not necessary for Canada to
DEBATES	6813

We need to have some kind of balance in our approach to this problem. I say that we cannot reduce inflation below a certain level. We should try to adjust our economy in the light of this fact. It is fairly obvious that most of the inflation from which Canada is suffering does not originate in this country. It comes from across the border, the United States. There is a very direct relationship between the rate of inflation in the United States and in Canada.
When hearings were held last summer concerning high interest rates, many witnesses appeared before the committee. If anything emerged from that committee hearing it was that as long as Canada is tied economically as tightly as it is to the United States, there is very little we will be able to do about inflation. Our situation is far worse than the American situation. We have a higher rate of inflation and a far greater degree of unemployment. The impact from across the border has had a multiplier effect in Canada.
One measure for controlling inflation that we should study is a way of making our economy somewhat less reliant on the United States. An inflationary tendency is built into our society. There is a movement from one sector of the economy to another. People are moving from the goods producing sector into the service sector. For a long time those in the service sector have received, generally, low wages. Adjustments will be necessary. On the whole, both the farming sector and the goods producing sector have been able to match wages with real increases in production; they have been able to increase productivity almost at the rate by which wages have increased. This is not true of the service sector, which means there will be an attempt on the part of those employed in it to catch up with those employed in the good producing sector. This, in itself, tends toward inflation in the long run.

It is often argued that Canada will price herself out of world markets unless a determined stand is taken against rising costs in this country. This is believed, I imagine, because there is an element of truth in it. One must examine it to find out how great is this element of truth, or whether the contention is true at all. I believe it is true only because of the somewhat senseless policy Canada has followed by establishing a fixed exchange

. Consumer Purchasing Power and Inflation rate. One way of exercising greater control over inflation and over our future plans would be to permit the exchange rate to float, as it did for many years before the government was panicked into fixing it.
There are a number of choices before us.
: The first is to try to live with inflation, 'making adjustments in old age pensions, veterans pensions and the returns of those living on fixed incomes-simply to go ahead with a full employment policy while learning to live 'with the problem. This is not the solution I am suggesting but it is certainly better than the policy the government is now adopting. Alternatively, and this is the course my party has been suggesting for a long time, the government should bring in an incomes policy. I should like to make it very clear what is meant by the term "incomes policy". An incomes policy is a way of allocating resources and making value judgments outside the marketplace-the Canadian people consciously deciding what the rewards of society should be and to whom they should go; it would not depend on whom could squeeze the hardest in the marketplace.
This does not mean all prices and wages have to be fixed. It means you have to be conscious of the problem and move in many different directions in order to get some intelligent allocation of resources and rewards in our society rather than every dog for himself as we have now. It means that at a time of inflationary pressure when resources are being demanded everywhere, the government should decide what the social priorities should be and where investments should go. What is really involved is an organized plan for using the resources of a society. This is what must be done if a reasonable approach is to be found for dealing with inflation while maintaining a high level of employment. At the moment, neither of these approaches is being followed; we are certainly not moving toward a planned use of our resources. Instead, a cover-up known as the Prices and Incomes Commission has been brought into existence. Not having a policy of its own, the government has said: Set up a commission, and see what it can do. Well, the Commission is doing its best under the circumstances, but it has no guidelines to help it; it does not know where it is going, and by confusing everyone it is preventing Parliament from coming to grips with the essential problem.
It seems to me, therefore, that this chamber must continue to debate inflation, unemployment and ways of dealing with these issues.

Mr. Speaker, it is not without satisfaction that I take this opportunity to speak to the motion introduced by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Rodrigue). Perhaps it does not mean much to some people, but it is very important to us.
In only a few lines, this motion sums up the means to reform our economy while at the same time indicating its drawbacks. What is wrong with our economy? If it were well balanced and properly administered, we would not witness the disagreement and the dissatisfaction which prevail in Canada today.
What is the reason behind such dissatisfaction? It is because we have people who can no longer eat their three meals daily or dispel the concern they feel.
In a country with plentiful riches, it is not logical that 60 per cent of the population be undernourished and deprived of essential things. Considering the fact that the cost amounts to $386,280 and that the contract was awarded for $327,000, one readily understands that the company financing the home will pay the cost of four, while using only one and that during those 50 years there will be maintenance costs to keep it in good shape.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been a

number of interesting comments about the motion presented to the House by the Rallie-ment Creditiste. Many would consider that by economic standards that are widely accepted in virtually all modernized industrialized nations of the world, the motion represents an interesting but unfortunate contradiction in terms. The effect of taking further steps at this time of the type called for by the Rallie-ment Creditiste could well add to the inflationary pressures that continue to exist in the economy and about which they have expressed concern.
The government, of course, does want to promote the greatest possible increase in the real purchasing power of Canadians; in other words, to bring about the greatest possible increase in their standard of living. But it wants to do so, Mr. Speaker, without jeopardizing the stability and soundness of the Canadian economy. There cannot be an increase in the standard of living which is real and meaningful unless, at the same time, we have a stable and sound economy. And the increasing ability of Canadians to acquire the goods and services that would raise the quality of their life depends in a vital way on the ability of the economy to produce them. The inflationary spiral that we are now experiencing was set in motion, in the first place, when the demand for goods and services both in our own country and in a number of other nations began three or four years ago to outrun the capacity of the economy to supply these goods and services. Even though the demand for goods and services has gradually been brought into balance with supply, the inflationary pressures set in motion some time ago continue to reverberate throughout the economy.
Contrary to the implication of the Creditiste motion, personal incomes and consumer spending have continued to rise at a rapid rate. During 1969, personal incomes, including wages, salaries and earnings of unincorporated businesses and farmers increased by 10.5 per cent. Even after deducting personal direct taxes, the increase in the amount of disposable personal income amounted to some 8.2 per cent. The increase in consumer spending, however, exceeded this increase in personal incomes, rising by 9 per cent in 1969 over the level in the previous year. This was made possible because Canadians saved less than during the year before. In 1968, Canadians saved 7.6 per cent of their disposable income, but in 1969 the ratio of personal savings declined to 6.8 per cent. The result was that
May 11. 1970	COMMONS
not only was there a heavy demand for consumer goods and services but that proportionately less money was set aside by Canadians in the form of personal savings with which to help finance the capital investment that is a prerequisite for increasing the ability of the economy to produce more real goods and services.
I am informed there is little evidence to date indicating that there has been any significant slowdown in the rate of increase of personal incomes or of the personal spending of Canadians. On the contrary, if the recent Labour Department survey of wage developments in the first three months of 1970 is any indication, personal incomes are continuing to increase at a rapid rate, which in turn, I am informed, will likely lead to further substantial increases in consumer spending this year. The survey estimated that as of March 31, 1970, the average base rate of some 1.4 million workers under collective agreements covering 500 or more employees, excluding construction, stood at 8 per cent over the level of a year ago. In the previous 12-month period the increase was 7.3 per cent.
It could be suggested that if there are increases in wages and salaries as well as other elements of costs far in excess of the expansion of productivity, the effect would be to maintain the inflationary momentum of the economy with the increased costs leading in turn to increased prices for a wide variety of goods and services bought by Canadians as consumers.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The policy of the government has been to moderate the growth and demand for goods and services so as to prevent a new thrust to inflation and to encourage the present inflationary spiral to lose its momentum. At the same time, the government has also sought to counter possible adverse impacts of fiscal and monetary restraints on slow-growth areas through a variety of selective measures, including regional economic expansion and manpower training programs, public works and the special consideration for loans in less developed areas urged on chartered banks by the Bank of Canada. A number of longer term measures have also been adopted, aimed at increasing the capacity of the economy to produce goods and services. These supply policies take time to increase the productivity of the economy, which is the real foundation of our standard of living. As noted earlier,

If the government took steps of the kind called for by the Ralliement Creditiste, it would incur the severe risk of intensifying today's already strong inflationary pressures.
The hon. member for Prince Edward-Has-ings (Mr. Hees) made some interesting comments. I might observe, however, that most Canadians, if they heard them, would say that if the Conservative Party really had the solutions to Canada's actual and potential economic problems in the way put forward by the hon. member, why were they not used in the period in which that party was in power between 1957 and 1963? They would also ask why conditions were what they were in those years, with rates of unemployment far above what they are today. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings spoke of turning things around. I would not want to be unkind in speaking of the remarks of the hon. member, but if I wanted to be unkind I suppose I could say that the Conservative government of which he was a part seemed to turn the preceding prosperity before 1957 into a number of years of Conservative depression.

I have just listened with interest to the remarks made by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray). For a moment, I thought the party in power agreed with the motion introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Rodrigue), which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should take all necessary steps to increase consumer purchasing power to meet their needs and to improve the flow of goods in Canada through the use of techniques designed to check rising costs and combat inflation.
Up to now, no government member has risen in his place to express either his approval or disapproval of this motion, and after hearing the remarks made by the Minister without Portfolio, I feel he would have been better to follow his colleagues' example, because the arguments he put forward to refute those of the opposition are most ludicrous.
I regret to have to use such words to describe the minister's speech, but I believe he went to a lot of trouble to prove not only that his government is unable to fight inflation but that he and the government are apparently satisfied with the situation.
When my colleagues of the Ralliement Cre-ditiste made some suggestions, he said that his government had taken steps to combat inflation and ensure a high rate of employment in Canada. If those steps are the ones which led to the runaway rise of prices and the present very high rate of unemployment in Canada, they are highly ineffective, to say the least.
The Minister is repeating, in a different way perhaps, the very words spoken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on television a few days before Easter, when he was interviewed on the budget speech just brought down by the Finance Minister (Mr. Benson).
DEBATES	6831
Consumer Purchasing Power and Inflation Both of them told us that the steps taken to fight inflation had failed, but that they were being maintained just the same.
This means more or less: We don't know where we are heading, but let us go anyhow.
I do not think this is what Canadians expect from, their government or what they have a right to expect from a good government. What they want is prosperity, because we live in a rich country with abundant natural resources of all kinds. We practically do not have to resort to foreign countries to meet our essential requirements.
What Canadians clamour for, and we especially, of the Ralliement Creditiste, is prosperity which is not beyond our means. The Canadian citizen will only be prosperous if he gets an adequate income. The whole count-try will only be prosperous if the national income remains at a high level.
The tightening up and the freezing of capital bring about economic crises, and some experiences, especially those lived through since 1929, are not easily forgotten.
In order to maintain the national income at a high level, the purchasing power of the taxpayer must be high so as to enable him to meet the requirements of life. In other words, money must circulate freely, leaving in its wake profits and prosperity.
In his book entitled Stable Money, Eisler analyses that situation. Here are excerpts from that book.
It is obvious that the purchasing power of the consumer varies according to the total amount of money and credit available to him for foodstuffs and services for immediate consumption. Since the monetary unit makes it possible to buy variable quantities of goods, according as the average price of foodstuffs is high or low, the consumer's real purchasing power is equivalent to the total amount of his nominal monetary income over a given period of time, after deduction of his savings, multiplied by the reciprocal value of the retail sales price index, that is to say the purchasing power of the monetary unit.
If foodstuffs are to flow regularly from producer to consumer, the latter's purchasing power must represent the total monetary value of foodstuffs earmarked for immediate consumption and offered by producers during the same period. Such a state of tilings may be defined as the ideal or normal balance of national or world market. If, at some point, the purchasing power of consumers is greater that the means that industry or agriculture have to directly produce consumption goods, prices will increase and the prospects of profit will induce capital holders to increase their productive capacity by installing new machinery, by hiring more employees, thus allowing a further growth of consumer purchasing power.

Consumer Purchasing Power and Inflation
On the other hand, If the total amount of money available for the purchase of immediate consumption commodities is lower that the total value of goods offered by producers, prices will fall, production will be reduced and producers will abstain from expanding their plants or from increasing their staff, and this will further decrease the consumer's purchasing power.
Consequently, the conditions on the market of produced goods are entirely dependent on the situation of consumer goods. Both markets will be depressed and employment will generally decrease if not enough money is directed towards the second of those markets.
That book was written several years ago, and today again the same conditions exist. We are still in a depression, employment is ever decreasing. Consequently, the purchasing power of consumers is reduced.
In his motion, my colleague is precisely proposing to increase the purchasing power as a solution likely to solve the problem of poverty in Canada.
According to statisticians, the standard of living of nearly 25 per cent of the Canadian population is below the poverty line and those people are suffering from a lack of purchasing power.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Any new rise in the cost of living adds to their worries and to their destitution.
Members from the Ralliement creditiste and, before them, other Creditiste members have from time to time put forward proposals very similar to those I wish to make tonight. During the few minutes that I have left, I should like to explain the essence of Social Credit.
The object of the Social Credit's financial creed it to give all members of society, the liberty and security that the economic and social system should provide them with. To this end, instead of bringing down production to the level of the purchasing power, by destroying useful goods or limiting work, we should bring up the purchasing power to the level of our production capacity as regards useful goods.
In short, there should be a complete reversal of the present situation. As a matter of fact, this government has been doing the very opposite in trying to fight inflation. They tax the Canadian people in order to subsidize Western producers not to produce wheat. They set a penalty of $1.52 per cwt. in the case of the milk producers in the East and in other parts of Canada because they produce too much.
Industries are also penalized. They are almost forced to shut down thus taking away the consumer's purchasing power. Plants slow down or shut down because there is nobody to buy their production.
Such a situation has sprung up from the present system that is advocated by the Liberal party. Bringing down production to the level of the purchasing power, instead of lifting the purchasing power to the actual or potential production level, does not enable all Canadian citizens to satisfy their needs.
As for us, we advocate four major means to implement Social Credit. In the pamphlet entitled Le Credit social et la doctrine sociale de VEglise, one reads as follows:
1. The State must take over the control on the issue and volume of money and credit. The State could exercise that control through an independent commission empowered to achieve that object.
Some will perhaps accuse us of wanting to nationalize money or the banks. It is not so. Social Credit does not want to nationalize the banks; it wants to nationalize credit. I shall explain myself by resuming the quotation:
Two elements constitute real credit: the capacity to produce and the needs to be met. Those two elements are essential to real credit. But as producers and consumers make up, between them, the whole community, we can certainly deduct from that that real credit is common, is social in its origin; it belongs neither to the producers, nor the consumers, but to the common element, the community, the society of which each is a part.
And so, if real credit is social, if real credit is common, financial credit must in turn reflect real credit, and, also belong to society. It cannot be left in the hands of a few bankers who create and manipulate it as they wish, by issuing it in the form of loans with interest.
In this regard, let us go back to the speech of the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) in this House this afternoon. Indeed, he explained very well how bankers create and manipulate, according to their whims, the credit they grant with interest. I continue the quotation:
We then conclude that the creation of financial credit must not depend on the banks, but on the State or its agency, and the financial credit must be issued by the State or its representative.
In his book entitled "La Doctrine economique de 1'Eglise" (The Economic Doctrine of the Church), Dauphin-Meunier points out again the inconveniences of the creation of bank credit by private banks.
The contemporary commercial banks, he says, receive deposits only to re-use them; they borrow only to lend money, and they make loans only for production. The development of these operations which, since the beginning of the 20th century

May 11. 1970	COMMONS
are made only through accounting procedures, without the use of silver or paper money, has put in evidence the fact that banks have at their disposal a real new power, that which the Belgian economist Anciaux has called script money.
Such issues compete with or counteract in fact the privilege of central banks; besides, they give to commercial banks a considerable discretionary power since, if at the beginning it is a loan of the client to the bank which will allow the latter to make a loan to a third party, the use of this cover by cheque writing or transfer can in turn bring in new deposits. In England, it was revealed that nearly three quarters of the sums due by the banks to their clients are due to the banks by their clients, because those clients have borrowed those sums from the banks on one form or another.
There lies a serious risk of economic and financial rupture, of credit inflation. And the author of the book concludes then: The state is thus led to intervene in order to reduce the fluctuations of the cycle. It has to direct the distribution of bank credits in a manner consistent with the national public well; it has to nationalize credit.
I would like Mr. Speaker to endorse the guidelines given by Pope Puis XI in his Encyclical "Quadragesimo Anno" and I quote:
There are some categories of goods which may rightly be considered as set apart for the community and that is when the economic power they eventually bestow is such that it cannot be left into the hands of private individuals lest it should prejudice the common good.
It says further: "It si obvious that not only his wealth concentrated in our times but an immense power, a despotic economic distatorship is consolidated in the hands of a few, who often are not owners but only the trustees and managing directors of invested funds which they administer according to their own arbitrary will and pleasure."
This dictatorship is more forcibly exercised by those who, since they hold the money and completely control it, control credit also and rule the lending of money. Hence, they regulate the flow, so to speak, of the life blood whereby the entire economic system lives, and have so firmly in their grasp, the soul as it were, of economic life, that no one can breathe against their will.
This discretionary power is left today to private interests and we ask the government to retrieve it since it answerable to the people, whose business he is supposed to manage. That is why we ask the government to nationalize not the banks but the credit, in order to better adjust it to reality. That is all we want.
The government could more easily increase the purchasing power of the Canadian taxpayers if it used the third means I shall describe for the information of hon. members.
In fact, we say that the material resources of the nation represented by production constitute the basis of the credit money. This means that we do not ask the government or

Furthermore, the issuing of bank notes and the granting of credit should at all times correspond to the production so that a healthy balance is maintained between production and consumption. This balance would be ensured partially by means of a discount, the rate of which would necessarily fluctuate along with the value of production.
I would once again for the benefit of members and those who will have the opportunity to read the official report of the proceedings of the House of Commons explain what we mean by compensated discount.
If, for instance, a suit costs $80 and a merchant sells it to a buyer for $60, the latter is given a reduction of $20. Stores call this a discount.
This discount is equal to one-fourth of the price of the suit. Arithmetically, one would say that it is a 25 per cent discount.
Let us suppose that Mr. Dupont had $100. If he had paid the full price for the suit, he would have spent $80 and he would have only $20 left. Because of the discount, Mr. Dupont spent only $60 and still has $40, instead of only $20. He will still be able to buy $40 worth of goods instead of $20. That is why we say that the discount increases purchasing power.
Mr. Dupont's purchasing power is increased by $20. It is the same as if he had paid the full price and had been given $20. The discount is equivalent to a gift of money. However, to benefit from it, he must buy the merchandise on which a discount is offered.
The Creditistes are used to hearing about dividends and national dividends.
The national dividend is only money given freely to everyone. That is what Social Credit is advocating. The discount amounts to a dividend; it is not given to all but only to the buyer.
The effect of that discount on Mr. Dupont is the same as that of a dividend. In either case, he is given $20, but the impact on business is different.
When $20 is given directly to Mr. Dupont, he can spend it but he can also save it or speculate with it. However, in order to avail himself of the $20 discount, Mr. Dupont had to buy an $80 suit. The dividend is not tied

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for its kindness. I will try to conclude my explanation as quickly as possible.
In the business world as we know it today, discounts are granted to purchasers for various reasons. It is up to the dealer to decide whether or not a discount is to be granted. He claims that it is to the advantage of the purchasers. But this is doubtful since the dealer does not want to give anything for nothing. Indeed, he is prompted to give the discount for another reason: he sees something in it for himself or he wants to reduce a loss. As a matter of fact, the products that pile up could turn out to be a complete loss. Instead of losing everything, the dealer sells his products at a discount; the purchaser is happy with that and, as far as the dealer is concerned, without being fully satisfied, he is nevertheless less unhappy than if he had made no profit at all. Perhaps he did so in order to sell a greater number of suits. If a suit cost the dealer $50, he would have made a $30 benefit had he sold it for $80. When he sells it for $80, his profit is cut down to $10. On the other hand, if, having slashed his price, he sells five times more suits, his profit then is five times $10 instead of one time $300.
So, whatever are the reason for which the dealer grants a discount, he expects a negative or a positive compensation. He may not get it but he tries to. He makes every effort to get it. I just described the ordinary discount granted by ordinary dealers.
Let us deal now with Social credit, the credit for society.
According to the Social Credit, theory, the discount is national like the dividend, that is to say that the discount is general like the dividend. It is granted to every buyer of any consumer commodity just as the dividend is granted to every citizen without exception. As the discount is granted by the nation, it is the nation that has to see to the compensation so that the dealer should not suffer any loss. This is why the National Credit Board, 
the same which issues money to everybody as dividends, issues also money to dealers for the discounts they have to grant to buyers.
In selling the dress to Mr. Dupont at $60 the dealer looses $20. The National Credit Board which is responsible for the discount granted to Mr. Dupont must compensate it in sending to the dealer a cheque for $20. On what guarantee shall the National Credit Board draw this cheque for $20? On Canada's production capacity, exactly as it would be for a dividend. So the dealer will get the amount of $80 which he normally should have got. Mr. Dupont keeps the $20 extra. Therefore it is Mr. Dupont who will finally draw $20 more on Canada's production. The compensated discount is therefore the new money which has been given to the dealer, but in favour of the buyer. This assistance for the buyer increases the number of sales and we all know that today the dealer tries to sell more goods by granting discount.
In a creditiste regime, the dealer would get the same result without running risks and without reducing his profit on every item.
The compensated discount is therefore profitable to everyone. For the dealer, it is better than a dividend, because the latter can remain unapplied, while the discount has required a purchase of goods.
However, the dividend maintains also its importance, even from the dealer's point of view, because even if there are all kinds of discounts, when non-salaried people have no money, they do not purchase anything. Therefore, no discounts are given. Dividends create a basis for discounts and discounts tend to increase the purchasing power of dividends and salaries. A discount without dividend equals to a salary increase. It is insufficient in a world where progress reduces salaries continually.
A discount accompanied by a dividend constitutes also a salary increase. In short, it constitutes a dividend increase for everyone, whether they are salaried or not.
Mr. Speaker, why do we claim a national dividend and a compensated discount? Because in today industrial structure, as well as in the organization of services, whether public transportation or otherwise, they permit a very substantial production calling for increasingly low levels of labour.
As a result, in the face of our present affluence, the global wages of Canadians steadily decreases.
May 11, 1970

But although individuals receive less and less revenue in the form of wages, they are at least entitled to benefit by the wealth provided by machines, experience, new inventions and the present production.
That is why we suggest a distribution of national dividends and compensated discount, not derived from taxes, but created by the Bank of Canada reporting to the government and based on the production offered to Canadian consumers. In this spirit, we have brought forward the motion which is being debated tonight and from which I quote:
...Increase consumer purchasing power to meet their needs and to improve the flow of goods in Canada through the use of techniques designed to check rising costs and combat inflation.
In making those proposals, we still wonder how the Canadian people could have been so patient for years and tolerate such a system as the one we have now.
We see poverty in the midst of affluence. The Ralliement Creditiste is demanding once again that this affluence be made available to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House provides us with an opportunity to reflect seriously on today's economic and monetary system, while prompting members to look for positive solutions to the problem we are facing.
There was a time when all our efforts were concentrated on production. I have no intention of repeating what my colleagues from Abitibi and Beauce (Messrs. Laprise and Rodrigue) have said with such spirit about the theories of Social Credit, which I sincerely and fully endorse.
During the few minutes at my disposal, I should like to tell the House the difference between the long term policy of Social Credit and that of the present government, if it can be called a long term policy because the government has not even drafted a short term policy.
There was a time when all our efforts were concentrated on production. They helped industrialize the country, reduce sometimes considerable distances from coast to coast, create jobs and dominate natural elements.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
This was accomplished through human resources, technics and money, either scrip money or any other.

Consumer Purchasing Power and Inflation
We have succeeded so well that today we can say without fear that our productive capacity is endless. In other words, the problem lies somewhere else.
There is however a prejudice prevailing in Canada and in this house, that the greater our productivity, the greater our prosperity.
This notion was forced upon us in the course of our studies, at the university or here, in the house. It is a truth of the industrial period. In the post-industrial era, it becomes a prejudice which I must fight, because it is not true that the greater our productivity, the greater our prosperity.
It is precisely what the Creditistes are challenging, because even if production is continuously rising, poverty and destitution are also increasing. We see it every day.
In other words, a higher production does not necessarily eradicate poverty and injustice. The government, while advocating an increased production, is taking steps which are prejudicial to consumers. They are not selective measures based on his capacity to pay, in order to protect those who are unable to do so and try to distribute our created wealth, but fiscal, monetary and other measures applying uniformly to all. Finally only the very rich can manage at worst with a few scratches, while the underdog, the poor, the farmers, the workers, the unemployed, the social welfare recipients, the young are caught in government machinery and unable to extricate themselves.
However, the government retorts that there are social security allowances paid out of the taxpayers' money. Once again, the government deprives certain taxpayers of purchasing power to give it to other.
In this way, he reduces purchasing power by as much, so we are not any better off and the gap between the rich and the poor becomes wider.
That is why I enthusiastically support the motion of the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Rodrigue) which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should take all necessary steps to increase consumer purchasing power-
Mr. Speaker, what is the present policy of the Liberal Government and what was that of the Progressive Conservative government that preceded irt? Both advocate, first, increased production, second, restriction of purchasing power.
How does the government limit consumption?
Consumer Purchasing Power and Inflation By levying taxes. The purchasing power is thus removed without making any distinction between the one in a position to invest in Canada and the other who is not and, therefore, poverty increases in this wealthy country.
When the government of Quebec informs us, for instance, that it will create 100,000 jobs, does it really solve the economic problem? No. And here is what the Creditistes are saying: it is very well to create jobs but a guaranteed minimum income must also be provided to every Canadian citizen so that he may share in the national production.
We shall then have created a system likely to ensure some kind of economic justice to every Canadian.
When a youth, for instance, drops out of school for some reason or another, mostly for lack of money, he enters the labour market or rather, the unemployment market.
Today, our main industry is social welfare. It is the main one in Victoriaville, in the riding of Lotbiniere and elsewhere, in the ridings of the members opposite. I am surprised to note that they keep silent, that they do not participate in the debate. It would seem that, for them, the problem does not exist.
Mr. Speaker, the people on welfare are supported by the state. The government gives them pensions from the taxpayers' moneys. They do not contribute to production. They want to take part to it provided they do not have to pay back as income tax what they have already received in the form of pensions.
I suggest the government, whether it be liberal or conservative, has a long and a short arm. The long one reaches into the taxpayers' pockets. And the short one gives away money only to those who are close at hand. Of course, this is patronage.
According to the Social credit, the government should not be one-armed; it must be strong. Both its arms must be of the same length. One must go into every taxpayer's pockets and the other one must hand out national dividends, which would not come from debts and taxes. Thanks to the national dividend and to the compensated discount, we shall be able to give each citizen his share of national production and wealth.
We want a sound government and a healthy country, not a crippled country and a limping government. That is why I support this motion. And I hope that my honorable colleagues

who did not rise in the course of this debate, and I am thinking especially of the government members, will read at least the official report of the House of Commons, so that they might see the light, because it does not seem that they have a very great amount of brains.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 23 I directed a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube) with respect to the attitude of the government concerning the veterans charter. I asked immediately for the privilege of bringing this matter up further at the ten o'clock adjournment because on that occasion the Minister of Veterans Affairs replied that veterans benefits are a part of social legislation, not social welfare. The reason there has been further delay in discussing this matter is the absence of the Minister of Veterans Affairs from the country in connection with the conmemoration held in Holland recently of the end of World War II.
Unfortunately, I see the Minister of Veterans Affairs is not in the House tonight so I doubt that we will get a specific answer at this time. However, I will proceed to try to point out to the House and the veterans of this country why I am pursuing this matter at the present time and asking for something much more specific than the answer I received on April 23.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
There is a tendency on the part of the government to remove, not by direct action but rather by stealth and indirection, some of the traditional rights which we regard as the essential part of the veterans charter. I refer to action such as in the case of the dismissed commissionaires which took place at National

May 11. 1970

Museum just over a year ago, and the lay-offs in the civil service which seemed to deny the traditional right of the veterans' preference. Having heard from veterans associations, I know that the Canadian Corps, the War Amps, the Royal Canadian Legion and the National Council of War Veterans Associations have written directly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as well as to the Minister of Veterans Affairs to get a specific reply to this vital question on the present status of the veterans charter. There has been no reply to those letters.
So that there will be no mistake as to what we mean by veterans charter, I shall read a few excerpts from a book entitled "Rehabilitation-A Combined Operation," published by the Department of Veterans Affairs, which lays down the basic background of the veterans charter. I shall first read from chapter 1, the heading of which is "Facing the Problem." It outlines the program and says:
It Is regarded as a preferred charge on the country's reserve; an obligation that must be fulfilled; part of the cost of freedom. .. there is a preponderance of opinion that strongly favours generous. . .treatment for exservicemen.
At page 9 the question is asked:
"What should the country do in an endeavour, so far as this can reasonably be done, to replace the years 'that the locust hath eaten'? What does the country owe to those who, forsaking everything, offered their lives in its defence-to try and compensate for the time that was lost and the opportunities that were missed?"
At page 10 the answer is given:
One soon reaches the conclusion that in many, many cases it is impossible to compensate the veteran for all he has lost. For those who have1 suffered injury or disease the best that the state can do is to provide medical and surgical treatment in an endeavour to restore the individual, as far as science can, to the maximum of his capacity and, when this is done, to provide compensation for whatever residual disability remains.
I submit that there is the essence of the veterans Magna Carta. I further suggest that when the minister says in an answer that veterans rights are now considered as social policy, rather than on the basis of the traditional veterans charter, this is a further erosion of the special rights of those men and women who served their country. I hope that tonight we get a definitive answer to the question: Does the veterans charter still stand as it was outlined in the book published by the Department of Veterans Affairs in 1953, or is it now a part of Canada's general social welfare policy?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 17 I put the following question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson):
In view of the minister's statement on television over the weekend that unemployment will De higher in 1970 than it was in 1969, can the minister assure the House that high unemployment areas such as the Maritimes, eastern Quebec and the Prairies will not suffer from even higher unemployment in 1970 as a result of the government's anti-inflation policies.
It is nearly two months since I put that question. The statistics now before us point out very clearly that regionally-depressed areas such as those I have mentioned are indeed suffering higher unemployment. Per-

DEBATES	May 11, 1970
haps I can spend two minutes to compare the unemployment rate in the three areas with what it was three years ago. In 1963, in the Maritimes, unemployment was 10.6 per cent of the work force. In March, 1970, it was 10.8 per cent. The same thing in Quebec-in 1967, 7.2 per cent of the labour force was unemployed and three years later in March, 1970, it was 9.2 per cent. This is for the entire province of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, not just for the depressed areas and the eastern part of the province. On the Prairies the unemployment rate jumped from 2.7 per cent to 5.2 per cent in the same three-year period. A province such as Saskatchewan is harder hit because it is more dependent than Alberta, say, in respect of agriculture and the wheat industry. Even those bare statistics point out that these areas are being hit harder than most other parts of Canada. Because of the government's anti-inflationary policy more people are unemployed proportionately in these areas than in other parts of Canada.
Looking back over the last election campaign there seems to be quite a contradiction in the main issue expressed then by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He talked about national unity and about correcting regional inequalities and disparities. It seems to me there are more regional disparities today than there were two or three years ago before this Prime Minister came into power. More people in the provinces are unemployed now than there were three years ago. The whole economy of Saskatchewan has slowed down in the last three years. This is a very serious problem of which the government must take heed.

It says in effect that the farmer will have to make a declaration. Then it says that where any information is given-
[DOT]-the information shown in that permit book shall, in the absence of evidence satisfactory to the Minister to Agriculture to show that the information was incorrect, be deemed to be correct for the purposes of the application.
The minister should state fairly, frankly and honestly the rules of the game. A previous document stated there would be an inspection. The official document which was tabled recently states something quite different. Now we get another officially-tabled document which says something quite different.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
The livelihood of a great many farmers depends on how well this operation is carried out. Goodness knows, they will be penalized enough because the operation will reduce income generally in western Canada. But at least the process should be clearly defined 
and well set out so that everyone would know what the regulations are, how they will be carried out and what rights the farmer will possess. He needs to know. If the department releases a flock of inspectors, many of them ill-informed and ill-trained, the farmer had better know what his rights are so that he can protect himself from absence of information or plain clumsiness on the part of inspectors.
The heading in the last issue of the Western Producer reads, "Chaos in Marketing Feared". The reference is to the board of directors of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool in the event that extra delivery points are opened up. This is a no-man's land which the farmers and the people generally are facing in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has managed to ask a number of questions in the time available to him and I am not sure I will be able to do them justice in the few minutes allotted to me. If he looks back to the original question he asked on April 17 and the answer he received from me to the effect that the question of how the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) might be satisfied on the subject of the removal of the cover crop was in the process of being determined, he will realize that we were in fact considering at that time a possible change or modification so as to give greater flexibility in the way in which the removal of cover crops could be assumed.
The regulations have specified that the minister must be satisfied. This flexibility has been provided because until the exact number of acres under cover crops is known, it is not known which method might be required to ensure that farmers have complied. This is of no concern to farmers who will comply, because the system will be suitable for them; it is only for those who might be inclined not to comply, and this is bound to be a very small proportion.
As far as the question of measuring acres is concerned, it is our intention that use shall be made of aerial surveys. This will make possible a fairly good assessment of the indications which farmers have given in their application forms. Inspections may be required in cases of gross breach; special measures may be required. Again, there should be no fear on the part of farmers ordinarily complying with the program.
The hon. member seems to think we have made some change in the way in which pay-
